transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-12-05
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Ava Gomez (Redwood SE), Priya Narang (CTO, Quantify Labs), Elena Park (ML Infra Lead), Marcus Chen (SRE), Diego Alvarez (Inference Engineer)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Samir: Quick dive on kernel selection and why we saw the NV jitter; walked through CUDA graph captures, pointed out kv cache warmup pattern causing throughput drop, discussed vLLM's scheduling versus TensorRT-LLM fused kernels. Agreed to share traces and run pilot on Quantify's VPC.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we have a full table, I'll hand it over to Samir to kick off the deep dive.
[00:10] Samir: Thanks Jordan. Hi Priya, Elena, Marcus, Diego. Today we wanna go through the profiling we ran on the YXZ family models and talk about kernel selection differences between TenSORRT-LLM and vLLM, and then show a couple CUDA graph captures. I know you sent some perf numbers, Diego, so we'll reference those.
[00:28] Diego: Yep, thanks. I put the raw numbers in the sheet we shared, there might be a couple of mismatched rows, apologies — I exported from our internal test runner.
[00:36] Samir: No problem, that's fine. Quick call out: some terms might get munged by the autotran script; KV cache sometimes shows up as "KV cash" in the trace export, so if you see weird words that's likely the thing.
[00:47] Elena: Haha, yes saw that. Also we hit a weird tail latency spike when we tried batching of 8 on sequence length 2048.
[00:54] Samir: Right, that's the pattern we'll dig into — it's a mix of kernel launch variance and prefix cache filling.
[01:05] [01:05] Jordan: Before deep dive — what are your success criteria for this call? Are we trying to pick a runtime for pilot or just debug the profiling?
[01:13] Priya: Both. Top priority is stable p99 latency under our peak workload. Second is per-token cost. We want to see whether Dedicated Redwood or running in our VPC with TensorRT-LLM is the best starting point.
[01:26] Samir: Cool. We'll frame the tradeoffs with numbers and show where kernel selection matters.
[01:30] [02:00] Samir: Ok first slide — kernel selection. vLLM uses a lot of fused kernels in the FWD path but relies on cuBLAS for matmuls; TensorRT-LLM compiles fused attention and uses custom kernels for softmax/scale and gelu. The difference shows up in sequence lengths where attention memory layout changes. We captured two traces to illustrate.
[02:20] Marcus: On our side we saw that vLLM had slightly higher single-request latency but better throughput under heavy batching, is that consistent?
[02:29] Samir: Yeah that aligns — vLLM's scheduler is more flexible, it can overlap different requests and keep warps busy; TenSORRT-LLM's compiled kernels push lower per-token compute but sometimes suffer from kernel launch overheads and less dynamic batching.
[02:45] Diego: We noticed when sequence length jumped from 512 to 2048, TenSORRT-LLM throughput dropped unexpectedly. Is that an indexing or kv cache issue?
[02:56] Samir: It's often a kernel selection threshold; the runtime picks an alternate attention kernel at larger seq len which uses a different memory layout, also the KV cache warmup behavior can create a short period where memory copies are blocking.
[03:10] Ava: We profiled with CUDA graphs and saw the capture included a bunch of memcpy H2D calls during first steps — that suggests not all allocations were captured in the graph and some fallback paths got hit.
[03:23] Elena: We definitely saw memcpy spikes in the early prefixes. Could that be our input pipeline? We stream prompts from S3 and do some pre-tokenization in the host.
[03:30] Samir: That's plausible — if the host-side preproc is not pinned memory or you're staging data differently, the CUDA graph capture might not include those host transfers. We recommend pre-allocating pinned buffers and warmup runs prior to capture.
[03:42] [04:00] Samir: I'll show the first CUDA graph — note the timeline: kernels A,B,C fused attention, then memcpy, then kernel D. The memcpy sits between two fused kernels which reduces overlap and causes a short tail.
[04:15] Diego: Is that memcpy coming from KV cache writes? It looked like an H2D for the cache.
[04:21] Samir: Could be. Our nvprof annotation shows some of the memcpys labeled as kv write; but sometimes the label is wrong — nvprofnaming is imperfect.
[04:29] [05:00] Priya: From an infra POV we also need to understand why the p99 jumps with batching in VPC. Is network a contributor?
[05:10] Samir: Network can add variance if your model is on a remote NVMe mount or you have container image pulls, but for steady-state inference it's usually the kernel scheduling and fallback to non-captured paths. We saw the VPC-run had slightly higher variance because their instance used a mixed CPU affinity config.
[05:26] Marcus: We used r5 cores pinned to the containers, but we didn't pin IRQs — could that matter for GPU scheduling?
[05:33] Samir: It can. IRQ and CPU affinity affects the threads that enqueue work to the GPU. If those threads get descheduled you can see gaps. We recommend isolating the enqueue cores and using thread pinning for low-p99 requirements.
[05:48] [06:00] Ava: Back to kernel selection — an interesting datapoint: when we forced TensorRT-LLM to use cuBLAS for certain matmuls (via config override) we saw smoother latency but slightly worse throughput. That indicates fused kernels are optimal for throughput when aligned, but they can introduce more variability when their heuristics misfire.
[06:18] Diego: How about quantization — we tested int8 and saw a 20% throughput win but occasional hallucination of answers changed. Is that expected?
[06:27] Samir: Yes quantization affects numeric stability for norm/scaling. Some ops are quant-sensitive; we often recommend mixed-precision or calibration on a representative prompt set. Also watch for kernel implementations that replace a fused op with an approximate op under quantization.
[06:42] [07:00] Jordan: On the product side — for a pilot, would you recommend running Redwood Dedicated or deploying TensorRT-LLM in their VPC? Quick pro/cons?
[07:09] Samir: Short answer: Dedicated if you need predictable latency and we provide SLA; VPC if you need full network isolation and control of driver/kernel stacks (e.g., custom CUDA drivers). For initial profiling, VPC pilot is useful because you can reproduce your production env; Redwood Dedicated pilot can be provisioned after we tune the config.
[07:27] Priya: We have some compliance constraints — needs KMS integration and audit logs, so VPC looks appealing.
[07:33] Jordan: We can support KMS and audit logs in both Dedicated and Private, we'll share the whitepaper.
[07:39] [08:00] Samir: Now show a compare trace: vLLM timeline vs TensorRT-LLM. Notice vLLM keeps many smaller kernels but overlaps copies with compute; TenSORRT-LLM has larger fused kernels and sometimes serialization at kernel boundaries.
[08:20] Elena: The vLLM overlap looked great, but we did see higher GPU memory footprint with vLLM. Is that typical?
[08:28] Samir: Yes vLLM's dynamic scheduling and workspace allocations can be more memory-hungry. If you're memory constrained, TensorRT-LLM's fused kernels and workspace pooling can be more compact.
[08:40] Diego: There's also the KV cache strategy — vLLM keeps per-request cache pointers optimized for multi-tenancy, whereas TensorRT-LLM prefers contiguous cache layouts for performance. Which one maps better to our multi-tenant inference?
[08:55] Samir: For multi-tenant, vLLM's approach reduces memory fragmentation but may limit peak single-tenant throughput. If your workload is dominated by a few heavy tenants, contiguous layout with Redwood's prefix cache can be faster.
[09:10] [09:30] Marcus: Any tips for capturing clean CUDA graphs? We tried capture and results were non-deterministic across runs.
[09:38] Samir: Key tips: 1) Use persistent allocations and pinned host buffers, 2) run warmup iterations to fill KV cache and allocate workspaces, 3) ensure no dynamic allocation during capture path, 4) set CUDA stream/launch flags consistently. Also watch for non-capturable APIs (some allocator wrappers cause fallbacks).
[09:54] Diego: We saw one run where the trace captured an occasional cudaLaunchKernel fallback — how do we avoid that?
[10:01] Samir: That usually means the kernel chosen wasn't available for capture or the runtime selected a fallback path because of an unsupported device capability. Make sure you're on the expected driver/arch and that the TensorRT plugins are compatible.
[10:13] [11:00] Ava: On batching: we recommended continuous batching for low-latency workloads; we saw Quantify's tail jumps when batching to 16. The right batch size depends on seq length distribution and p99 target. Smaller batches often help p99 while slightly hurting throughput.
[11:29] Priya: Our workload has bimodal seq len (64 tokens for chat and 2048 for doc). What's the recommended strategy?
[11:37] Samir: Use route-based policies: keep short chat on low-latency pool with small batch size and doc requests on a throughput pool or use model variants (quantized) for doc paths. Also prefix caching for doc flows reduces repeated compute.
[11:54] Diego: Regarding prefix caching — we had a case where cache invalidation caused recompute more often than expected. Any patterns?
[12:02] Samir: Common issue: tokenization differences or prompt templating causing cache miss due to whitespace or invisible char differences. Normalize prompts before hashing cache keys and provide a canonicalizer in the client.
[12:17] [12:30] Jordan: On the audit/compliance note — how much of this profiling and kernel choice is driver-dependent? If Quantify wants on-prem with older drivers will that break things?
[12:38] Samir: It can. TensorRT-LLM compiled engines can be sensitive to minor driver changes. That's why in Private deployments we recommend a managed compatibility matrix and pinned driver images. vLLM is more forgiving but may be slower.
[12:52] Elena: For our VPC pilot we'll likely be on Ubuntu 22.04 and driver 540. Are those in Redwood compatibility matrix?
[12:58] Jordan: We'll attach our compatibility matrix and check; Samir will note any driver-specific kernels that require 545+.
[13:08] [13:30] Samir: Quick detour — we profiled quantized kernels: int8 gives good throughput but watch layerwise degradation. We often run a calibration pass with representative prompts to avoid large accuracy drops. Also watch the custom softmax kernel behavior under int8 — some approximations can skew logits under long contexts.
[13:48] Priya: Calibration tooling — do you provide tooling or do we need to run our own?
[13:54] Samir: We have a calibration helper in our Optimize toolkit; we can run calibration on your sample prompts during the pilot. We'll share a script that produces calibration tables.
[14:05] Diego: About batch scheduling — would Redwood runtime be able to dynamically switch between vLLM-like scheduling and TRT compiled mode?
[14:13] Samir: Our routing can pick model variants; runtime can route requests to a vLLM pool or TensorRT-LLM pool and we have fallback policies. But switching within a single GPU process between scheduler modes is non-trivial. We usually run separate pools optimized for each pattern.
[14:29] [15:00] Marcus: Any gotchas for VPC/on-prem around KMS/HSM integration when using pinned kernels? For example does KMS add latency to each token?
[15:09] Ava: KMS is usually for key sealing of persistent artifacts (e.g., model encryption at rest); runtime unwrap happens at boot or session start, not per-token. But if you design per-request encryption that requires frequent KMS calls you will add latency. We typically support local key caching & HSM attestation patterns.
[15:29] Priya: Good. For our security team we need to confirm support for an HSM-backed KMS and audit trails.
[15:36] Jordan: We'll share the Private deployment security docs and SOC2; Elena can confirm.
[15:43] [16:00] Samir: Returning to CUDA graphs — we recommend capturing two graphs: one for short sequences and one for long sequences. For mixed workloads you may need two engine variants. Also check that graph capture includes all memory allocations to avoid fallbacks.
[16:16] Diego: Capture size exploded when we tried 2048 steps, the graph file was several GB. Any tips?
[16:23] Samir: Use pruning: only capture the steady-state region, not the entire scroll of steps. Also use graph partitioning for very long context models.
[16:34] Priya: Any changes we should expect if we upgrade to A100->H100?
[16:40] Samir: H100 has better sparsity and improved tensor cores; kernel choices may change. Some plugins optimize better on H100 so you might see throughput wins, but also different numerics. We'll run the same traces on H100 for apples-to-apples.
[16:55] [18:00] Ava: I want to call out a small engineering note: when using TensorRT-LLM fused kernels, verify that your model's layernorm placement matches the fused kernel expectation. Mismatched ops result in kernel fallbacks.
[18:13] Diego: We had mismatch due to custom layernorm implementation from a forked HF model. Is rewriting necessary?
[18:20] Samir: Often small shim layers or conversion fixes fix it. We'll include a checklist for model export compatibility.
[18:31] [20:00] Jordan: Let's talk timeline for the pilot. Priya, what are you thinking?
[20:07] Priya: We want to get something running in the next two weeks, ideally a VPC pilot to validate p99 under chat load and throughput for doc workloads. If that looks good we can evaluate Dedicated in January.
[20:18] Jordan: Sounds reasonable. We'll aim to have the initial artifacts to you within 3 business days.
[20:25] Samir: Action items recap: Samir shares traces, Diego shares model + prompts, Jordan shares pricing + security docs. Also we'll set a follow-up 1hr pilot kickoff next week.
[20:40] Elena: Quick question — during our test we saw nvlink bandwidth occasionally saturate causing cross-GPU copies to slow. Does Redwood have suggestions?
[20:49] Samir: For cross-GPU workloads we prefer model sharding that minimizes cross-GPU KV transfers and use NCCL tuned for your topology. Also topology-aware scheduling helps. We'll include a short note.
[21:05] [21:30] Priya: Thanks, this was helpful. One last: can you share the raw flamegraphs and the small benchmark harness we can run in our VPC?
[21:39] Samir: Yes, we'll share the harness and flamegraphs; they live in the profile folder we shared earlier (link: https://redwood.example.com/profiles/quantify/2025-12-05). Note that link may require auth.
[21:52] Diego: Perfect. We'll try to run the harness this week.
[22:00] [22:30] Jordan: Great. Any other points?
[22:34] Marcus: Nothing else from infra.
[22:37] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[22:40] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and schedule the pilot kickoff.
